source.title: Lower Bounds on the Generalization Error of Nonlinear Learning Models

record.tranche_reason: The paper varies the training-sample ratio and plots the SGD-trained networks' generalization error, conceptually testing whether more data can change test error. It does not use a direct double-descent analysis.
record.gate_note: Figures 5 and 6 plot SGD generalization performance against γ0=d/M, so the sample-size results are relevant to V3. The plotted bounds are lower bounds, not measured test errors, and were not recorded as rows. The text cites double-descent findings from other work; those cited results were not recorded.
record.test_reason: The paper derives Cramér–Rao-type lower bounds on generalization error for two-layer networks and compares them with SGD in a teacher–student setup. The body text never discusses double descent. The double-descent papers (1812.11118, 1912.02292, Mei & Montanari) appear only in the reference list. The SGD curves against γ0=d/M are plotted only as a benchmark for the bounds. The authors never interpret them as test error rising or falling around an interpolation threshold. The student has about 5,000 first-layer parameters (100×50) plus 100 output weights, so it would interpolate near M≈5,000 (γ0≈0.01). That lies at the extreme left edge of the plotted γ0 range of 0–4, so the sweep cannot show a sample-wise peak near interpolation. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors derive Bayesian Cramér–Rao lower bounds for any estimator of a two-layer network in the proportional regime, and show the bound is tight for linear activation. Numerically, SGD performance respects the bounds, even under a uniform weight prior. They argue that unbiased estimators perform badly for nonlinear networks, because the expected rank of the Fisher information is about β1·d². They draw no conclusion about double descent.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives generalization lower bounds and compares them with SGD performance; it does not reproduce the original double-descent experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The plotted SGD settings vary activation function, noise variance, teacher weight prior, student hidden-unit count, and sample ratio.
record.problems: The relevant sample-ratio outcomes appear only in plots; the text provides no numerical test-error values or interpretation of the curve shapes.
record.rows_left_out: The trivial mean predictor and bias curves in Figures 5 and 6 were not included because they are not the SGD network's test generalization error. The displayed lower-bound curves were excluded because they are theoretical bounds rather than measured test errors.

untested.parts: No sweep of test error over model size. Figure 4 varies hidden width only for the theoretical bounds.
No test error tracked over epochs; SGD is fixed at 100 epochs.
The sample-size sweep does not probe the student's interpolation threshold, and the curve shapes are not described.
Two noise levels are shown only as benchmarks. There is no analysis of a peak, multiple descent, or tuned regularization.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's guess of tests/T2 is wrong. The γ0=d/M axis is not the student's interpolation axis: γ0=1 marks M=d (linear-regression style), not M equal to the parameter count. The only behaviour discussed at γ0=1 (Remark 3.2) concerns the theoretical lower bound in the high-SNR limit, not measured test error.

versions.untested_parts: No test-error sweep over model size.
No test-error results over training epochs; the SGD runs use 100 epochs.
The figures plot test generalization error against d/M, but the text does not describe the curve's shape or report extractable values for behavior near the interpolation threshold.
No general double-descent curve across model classes is tested.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location.
The paper compares two noise variances in one figure but does not test peak mechanisms, multiple descent, or optimally tuned regularization.
No re-counting of complexity or test of whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.
